title: Aggregation and the newer LINQ operators
body: Aggregates reduce a sequence to one value: `Count`, `Sum`, `Average`, `Min`, `Max` and the general `Aggregate(seed, (acc, x) => ...)`. `Min`/`Max`/`Average` on an empty sequence of non-nullable numbers throw `InvalidOperationException`; check `Any()` first, or use `DefaultIfEmpty` or a nullable projection.

Element operators pick one item: `First`/`Last`/`Single` throw when nothing (or, for `Single`, more than one item) matches; the `OrDefault` variants return default, and since .NET 6 accept the default value to use. `MaxBy`/`MinBy` return the element with the largest or smallest key rather than the key itself.

Set-like and shaping operators: `Distinct`, `DistinctBy(key)`, `Union`, `Intersect`, `Except` (with `...By` variants), `Chunk(size)` for batches, `Zip` for pairing sequences, `Take`/`Skip` and their `While` forms, plus `Take(range)` such as `Take(^3..)`.

Newer operators replace common GroupBy patterns: `CountBy(key)` and `AggregateBy(key, seed, func)` (.NET 9) return key/value pairs without building groups, and `Index()` (.NET 9) pairs each element with its position. They are cheaper and clearer for frequency counts and per-key totals.
Before calling an aggregate, check what happens on an empty input and whether duplicates should count. Prefer `Any()` to `Count() > 0`, which may enumerate everything.

challenge: Given exam scores as (string Student, int Score) tuples with repeated students, print each student's best score using AggregateBy, sorted by student, and the overall top student using MaxBy.
question: What does `Average()` do on an empty int[]?
reasoning: Non-nullable Min/Max/Average have no meaningful empty result; project to a nullable type or check Any() first.
